blocks.title: Typical output (timestamps vary): C2 code is invalidated when Circle appears

blocks.text: Before "phase 1 done" `total` reaches tier 4 assuming every `Shape` is a `Square`. The moment a `Circle` arrives, the type check in the compiled code fails and both tier 4 versions are marked `made not entrant` at 219 ms. The method restarts in tier 3 (profiling again), and a new tier 4 version, compiled with the knowledge of both classes, appears 5 ms later. With `-Xlog:deoptimization=debug` you see the reason: `class_check`. Other causes: an `if` branch never taken before is taken, a class is loaded that invalidates an assumption (e.g. a new subclass overriding an inlined method), an unexpected null, or an array index out of range.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: A burst of deoptimisations right after start-up or after a deployment is normal. A steady stream of them in a long-running service is a clue that the program's behaviour keeps changing shape (a megamorphic call site or a flip-flopping branch).

### Microbenchmark traps

Because of warm-up, inlining and dead-code elimination, **hand-written timing loops usually measure the wrong** **thing**. Look at this loop, which looks like it measures the cost of `Math.sqrt`:

blocks.title: Bad.java

blocks.code:
$ java Bad.java
loop took 72 ms
loop took 102 ms
loop took 0 ms
loop took 0 ms
loop took 0 ms
blocks.title: Typical output on the build machine

blocks.text:
The "0 ms" is real: once C2 compiled the loop, it saw that the result is never used, that `Math.sqrt` has no side effects, and removed the whole loop (**dead-code elimination**). A hundred million square roots in under a millisecond is not a fast machine, it is no work at all. The first two rounds measured warm-up, the last three measured nothing.

The traps, in short:

- **Warm-up**: the first iterations run interpreted or C1 code. Discard them.
- **Dead-code elimination**: if the result is not consumed, the work may vanish. Consume results.
- **Constant folding**: inputs that are compile-time constants get computed at compile time.
- **Loop optimisation and OSR**: code in `main` behaves differently from the same code in a separately-called method.
- **GC and noise**: allocation rate, other processes, CPU frequency and, on a 2-CPU machine like this one, the JIT threads competing with your code.
- **Profile pollution**: running benchmark A before B changes the type profiles that B is compiled with.

The fix is a harness. **JMH** (Java Microbenchmark Harness, from the OpenJDK project) handles forks, warm-up iterations, measured iterations and a `Blackhole` that consumes results so the JIT cannot discard them. It is a separate dependency, so it is shown here as text only (not run in this book):

blocks.title: SqrtBenchmark.java (JMH, not run here)

blocks.text: Generate a project from the JMH Maven archetype (`org.openjdk.jmh:jmh-java-benchmark-archetype`), build the benchmark jar and run `java -jar target/benchmarks.jar`. Read the score together with its error margin; compare two variants only under identical settings. The performance chapter in the design Part repeats the rule: measure first, with a real tool.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not decide between two implementations from a `System.nanoTime()` loop in `main`. Either use JMH or measure the whole application under realistic load with a profiler or JFR.

### Flags, code cache and the cost of warm-up

You rarely need JIT flags, but know what they are:

rows: Log each compile and invalidation (as above).
Interpreter only; shows the cost of no JIT. Never for production.
Use C1 only: faster start-up and lower CPU/memory, lower peak speed. Used for short-lived tools and some test runs.
Size of the code cache (251658240 bytes, 240 MB, on this machine with tiered compilation).
Number of compiler threads (2 here, chosen from the CPU count).
blocks.caption: JIT-related flags worth knowing.

blocks.text:
The **code cache** is a native memory region that stores compiled code. If it fills up (reported in the log as `CodeCache is` `full. Compiler has been disabled`) the JVM stops compiling new methods and the application slows down permanently. This is rare in modern JDKs, which flush cold code, but it can bite programs that generate lots of classes.

Warm-up costs real money in two situations. **Short-lived processes** (command-line tools, serverless functions) may finish before C2 does any work. **Autoscaled and restarted services** pay the warm-up on every new instance, sending production traffic to code that runs at a fraction of its eventual speed; a gradual load-balancer ramp-up (or a small synthetic warm-up request set) helps.

### Class Data Sharing, AOT and native images

Start-up has another cost: loading, verifying and parsing hundreds of classes. **Class Data Sharing (CDS)** stores the parsed, ready-to-use form of classes in a memory-mapped archive. The JDK ships an archive for its own classes (the log line `Opened archive .../classes.jsa` earlier in this Part's logs is exactly that). **Application CDS** adds your classes. On JDK 21 a *dynamic archive* is created at exit of a normal run (the classes must come from a jar):

blocks.code:
$ jar cfe warm.jar Warm Warm.class
$ java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=warm.jsa -jar warm.jar
$ java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=warm.jsa -Xlog:class+load -jar warm.jar | grep "Warm "
[0.041s][info][class,load] Warm source: shared objects file (top)
blocks.title: Application CDS on JDK 21

blocks.text:
The last line shows our class loaded from the shared archive. (When we ran the same experiment with a loose `.class` directory, the JVM printed `Skipping Warm: Unsupported location`; archived classes have to come from a jar or modules file.) Since JDK 19, `-XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa` creates and refreshes the archive automatically.

CDS shortens loading, not warm-up of the JIT. The newer **AOT cache** work from Project Leyden goes further: Java 24 and 25 added ahead-of-time class loading and linking (JEP 483), command-line ergonomics for creating the cache (JEP 514) and method profiling stored in the cache (JEP 515), so a later run can start compiling hot code sooner, and Java 26 allows the object cache with any collector (JEP 516). These need JDK 24 and later, so they are described here but not run on the build machine. The point for an engineer: a training run produces an archive that makes the next start faster, without changing your code.

**GraalVM Native Image** takes the opposite approach: it compiles your whole application ahead of time into a standalone executable. Start-up is in milliseconds and memory is small, which suits serverless functions and CLI tools. The costs: a closed-world assumption (everything reachable must be known at build time, so reflection, proxies and resources need configuration), long build times, no JIT so peak throughput is usually lower than HotSpot for long-running services, and a different set of diagnostic tools. Frameworks like Spring Boot and Quarkus have first-class support. We mention it for completeness; the rest of the book uses the standard JVM.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why is Java code slow at the start and fast later? What is a JIT? The JVM first interprets bytecode while counting method calls and loop iterations. Hot code is compiled to machine code by C1 and then, based on a collected profile, by C2, which inlines and speculates (for example that a call site has one receiver type) and falls back to the interpreter through deoptimisation if an assumption fails. The cost is warm-up: early requests run slower. Because of this, benchmarks need warm-up and a harness such as JMH.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Java is fast because of runtime compilation, and slow at first for the same reason.

- Tiered compilation: interpreter, then C1 (tier 3, profiles), then C2 (tier 4, optimised); the thresholds are about 200 and 5,000 invocations.
- C2 speculates on the profile (inlining monomorphic and bimorphic calls) and deoptimises when it is wrong; `-XX:+PrintCompilation` shows both.
- Never trust a hand-rolled timing loop: warm-up and dead-code elimination distort it. Use JMH.
- To start faster use CDS or AOT caches; to remove the JVM entirely use GraalVM Native Image, at a cost in flexibility and peak throughput.
#### Objects in Memory

items.question: How many bytes does `class P { int x; int y; }` occupy on a default 64-bit HotSpot (compressed oops)? What about `class Q { long a; }`?
items.answer: `P` is 12 + 8 = 20, padded to 24. `Q` is 12 + 4 (gap, filled by padding because a `long` must be 8-aligned) + 8 = 24.

items.question: Why is a `new int[3]` 32 bytes and not 28?
items.answer: Header 12 + length 4 = 16, plus 12 bytes of data = 28, rounded up to the next multiple of 8, which is 32.

items.question: You raise `-Xmx` from 31g to 33g to "get more room" and the service holds fewer objects. What happened?
items.answer: Above about 32 GB compressed oops are disabled, so every reference grows from 4 to 8 bytes and object headers/arrays of references get larger.

items.question: What is wrong with the claim "escape analysis puts objects on the stack"?
items.answer: HotSpot does not allocate on the stack. It proves the object does not escape and scalar-replaces it: fields become locals or registers and the allocation vanishes.

items.question: `List<Integer>` with 1,000,000 distinct values versus `int[1_000_000]`: roughly how many bytes each on a default JVM?
items.answer: About 20 MB (16-byte `Integer` objects plus 4-byte array slots; values above 127 are not cached) versus about 4 MB (16 + 4,000,000 bytes).

blocks.text: #### Heap Structure and Reference Types

items.question: In which generation is a freshly allocated `new ArrayList<>()` placed, and what makes that allocation cheap?
items.answer: In eden (unless it is a huge object that goes straight to old). The allocation is a pointer bump inside the thread's TLAB with no locking.

items.question: Name three kinds of JVM memory that are not limited by `-Xmx`.
items.answer: Any of: Metaspace, code cache, direct buffers, thread stacks, GC bookkeeping, native library memory.

items.question: What does this print, and why? `var r = new WeakReference<>(new Object()); System.gc();` `System.out.println(r.get());`
items.answer: Almost always `null`: the object is only weakly reachable, so the collector clears it. The snippet is not guaranteed because `System.gc()` is only a hint, but with default HotSpot settings it does run a full collection.

items.question: A `WeakHashMap<Key, Value>` never shrinks although you drop all other references to the keys. What is the likely cause?
items.answer: A value (or something it reaches) holds a strong reference to its own key, so the key is never weakly reachable.

items.question: Why must a `Cleaner` action not be a lambda that uses `this`?
items.answer: The lambda captures `this`, which keeps the object strongly reachable from the Cleaner's registry, so it never becomes unreachable and the action never runs by GC.

items.question: What guarantee do soft references give, and what do they not guarantee?
items.answer: All soft references are cleared before the JVM throws `OutOfMemoryError`. There is no guarantee when, or in which order, they are cleared before that point, nor that they stay while memory is fine.

blocks.text: #### Garbage Collection Fundamentals

items.question: Which of these are GC roots: a local variable in `main`, a field of an object in the old generation, a `static` field, a running thread?
items.answer: A local variable in `main`, a static field and a running thread are roots. A field of an old object is not a root itself; it is only reachable if the old object is.

items.question: What does this print, and what does it show? `Object a = new Object(); WeakReference<Object> w = new` `WeakReference<>(a); a = null; System.gc(); System.out.println(w.get());`
items.answer: It prints `null` in the typical case: after `a = null` the object has only a weak path, so the full collection triggered by `System.gc()` clears it. It shows that reachability, not variable scope, decides.

items.question: Why is the cost of a copying collection proportional to live data, not to garbage?
items.answer: The collector copies only what it reaches from the roots; dead objects are never visited, and the whole from-space is released at once.

items.question: What is the card table for, and what would a young collection need to do without it?
items.answer: It records which old-generation regions had a reference written into them. Without it, each young collection would have to scan the entire old generation to find old-to-young pointers.

items.question: Explain "Reaching safepoint" versus "At safepoint" in a `-Xlog:safepoint` line.
items.answer: "Reaching safepoint" is the time to bring all threads to a stop; "At safepoint" is the time the operation (such as the GC) took while they were stopped.

items.question: Which of throughput, latency and footprint does a bigger heap usually improve, and which does it cost?
items.answer: It usually improves throughput and the frequency of pauses, at the cost of footprint (memory); a very large heap can also increase the length of a single full collection for non-concurrent collectors.

blocks.text: #### The Collectors

items.question: Your service runs fine on a 4-CPU VM but in a Kubernetes pod limited to 1 CPU its pauses behave differently. Why might this be (before Java 27)?
items.answer: With fewer than 2 CPUs the JVM is not "server-class", so it selects Serial instead of G1: a different collector with different pause behaviour.

items.question: What does a `Pause Young (Mixed)` line in a G1 log tell you has happened earlier?
items.answer: A concurrent marking cycle ran and finished (concurrent start, remark, cleanup), so G1 knows which old regions hold the most garbage.

items.question: Why does ZGC not use compressed oops, and what does the load barrier do?
items.answer: ZGC stores metadata bits inside the 64-bit reference (colored pointers), so references cannot be compressed. The load barrier checks those bits on every reference load and, if the object has moved, fixes the pointer, so mutators never see stale addresses.

items.question: What happens if you run `java -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -Xmx16m` against a program that allocates 1 GB in total?
items.answer: The program dies with `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` once 16 MB is used; Epsilon never reclaims.

items.question: A G1 log shows `Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause)` repeatedly. Name two likely causes.
items.answer: The heap is too small for the live set, or the allocation rate exceeds what marking and mixed collections can reclaim; humongous allocations fragmenting the heap and a late-starting marking cycle are also common causes.

items.question: In which direction does a larger `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` push throughput and pause length?
items.answer: A larger goal lets G1 do more work per pause: fewer, longer pauses and usually higher throughput.

blocks.text: #### Reading GC Logs and Tuning

items.question: What is the default maximum heap of a JVM on a machine with 16 GB of RAM and no flags?
items.answer: 25 percent of the memory, about 4 GB.

items.question: In this line, how much memory did the collection free and how long was the pause? `[2.5s][info][gc] GC(7)` `Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 900M->150M(1024M) 31ms`
items.answer: 750 MB freed (900M to 150M); the pause was 31 ms.

items.question: What is wrong with `-Xmx4g` in a container with a 4 GB memory limit?
items.answer: The heap is only part of the process: Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct memory and GC structures push the total above 4 GB and the container is killed by the OOM killer. Leave headroom or use `MaxRAMPercentage`.

items.question: Why does `-XX:+PrintGCDetails` not work on Java 17?
items.answer: It belongs to the pre-Java-9 logging system; since Java 9 you use unified logging, for example `-Xlog:gc*`.

items.question: After every collection the "after" figure is larger than the one before, and Full GCs begin. What do you conclude, and does raising `-Xmx` fix it?
items.answer: The live set is growing: a leak or an unbounded cache. A bigger heap only delays the failure.

items.question: You set `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=20` and throughput drops. Why?
items.answer: A tiny pause goal forces G1 to use small young generations and fewer old regions per mixed collection, so collections happen more often and GC overhead rises.

blocks.text: #### Memory Leaks and OutOfMemoryError

items.question: What is the difference between a memory leak in Java and in C?
items.answer: In C you leak by forgetting to free; in Java the object is still reachable (a forgotten reference), so the collector may not free it. The cause is a lingering reference, not a missing `free`.

items.question: The service log says `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` after each redeploy of a web application without restarting the server. What is the likely cause?
items.answer: A class loader leak: something (a `ThreadLocal`, driver, thread or static reference from a shared parent loader) keeps the old application's class loader reachable, so its classes are never unloaded.

items.question: Why does `BUFFER.remove()` in a `finally` block matter when `BUFFER` is a `ThreadLocal` and tasks run on a thread pool?
items.answer: Pool threads outlive the task, so the value stays reachable through the thread's map; the memory is held until the thread dies, which in a server is the life of the process.

items.question: What is wrong with `catch (OutOfMemoryError e) { retry(); }` as a general strategy?
items.answer: After an OOM, state may be half-updated and the retry will likely fail again; fix the cause, or fail fast and restart (`-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError`).

items.question: What does this print, and why? `Object[] a = new Object[Integer.MAX_VALUE];` under `-Xmx64m`.
items.answer: `OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit` (we ran it above on JDK 21): the length is above what the VM supports at all, regardless of heap.

items.question: You see `unable to create native thread`. Raising `-Xmx` makes it worse. Why?
items.answer: Thread stacks are native memory outside the heap; a bigger heap leaves less room for the process under the OS or container limit.

blocks.text: #### The JIT Compiler and Warm-Up

items.question: What do the tiers 0, 3 and 4 stand for, and what does a `%` in `PrintCompilation` output mean?
items.answer: Tier 0 is the interpreter, 3 is C1 with full profiling, 4 is C2 (fully optimised). `%` marks an on-stack replacement compile of a loop inside a method that is already running.

items.question: A benchmark loop calls `Math.sqrt(i)` 100 million times and ignores the result, and reports 0 ms. Why?
items.answer: After warm-up C2 sees that the result is unused and `Math.sqrt` has no side effects, and eliminates the loop (dead-code elimination). Consume the result, or use JMH with `Blackhole`.

items.question: What does "made not entrant" tell you?
items.answer: The compiled version still exists for frames already running it, but no new calls will enter it; it was replaced by a better version or invalidated by deoptimisation.

items.question: A call site `shape.area()` has seen `Square` and `Circle` only. A third class `Triangle` starts to appear. What may the JIT do, and what is the effect on speed?
items.answer: The type profile becomes megamorphic (three or more receivers), so the call falls back to a virtual dispatch that cannot be inlined, and a compiled version based on the old profile may be deoptimised. Result: a modest slowdown.

items.question: Name two situations where warm-up cost matters more than peak speed, and one mitigation for each.
items.answer: Short-lived command-line tools or serverless functions (use CDS or a native image, or `TieredStopAtLevel=1`); freshly started service instances behind a load balancer (ramp traffic up gradually, or warm up with synthetic requests).

items.question: What is the difference between CDS and the JIT, and between the JIT and GraalVM Native Image?
items.answer: CDS speeds up class loading with a pre-parsed archive and leaves execution to the JVM; the JIT compiles hot bytecode to machine code while the program runs. Native Image compiles everything ahead of time to a standalone executable without a JVM or JIT.
